title.en: Why are you here? Um … zu

summary.en: Explain a purpose and recognize why the final action comes last.

body.en:
*Ich bin hier, um Geld zu verdienen.* — “I’m here to earn money.” The construction *um … zu* states a purpose. The word *um* opens the purpose part, and *zu* appears before the final action word: *um Geld zu verdienen*. The object, *Geld*, comes before that final pair.

The understood person is the same in both parts: Titus is here, and Titus intends to earn. The purpose part does not repeat the subject. This pattern is useful when the person responsible for the action is already understood from the main statement.

*Aber ich bin nicht hier, um Freunde zu finden.* — “But I’m not here to make friends.” The opening word *aber* marks the contrast without changing the ordinary order of the following main statement. The negative appears before the comma; it tells us that making friends is not his reason for being here.

*Freunde finden* is literally “find friends”; idiomatic English normally says “make friends”. That English choice belongs to this combination. It does not make the German word for finding a general replacement for every use of English “make”.

Keep the small words separate in the word drawer. Here *um* signals purpose and *zu* marks an infinitive. Translating the first as “around”, or treating the second as a destination, would give the wrong meaning in these sentences.

A new practice sentence is *Ich bin hier, um Freunde zu finden.* — “I’m here to make friends.” It uses the scene’s words to state a different purpose positively. It is a practice example, not a claim that Titus changes his mind. Compare it with the negative source statement, then replay his actual earning-money explanation.
